summary: The book of Susanna tells, as an independent story, what this Bible also preserves as Daniel 13: the beautiful and God-fearing Susanna, wife of Joakim in Babylon, is trapped in her garden by two elders appointed as judges. When she refuses them, they bear false witness, and the assembly condemns her. As she is led to death, praying 'O everlasting God, that knowest the secrets,' God raises up the young Daniel, who separates the witnesses and breaks their testimony on the name of a tree. The innocent is saved; the judges die by their own intended measure.
whyItMatters: Susanna is one of the oldest stories in the Bible about a woman believed over her own word — and about what due process owes the accused. Its heroine's sentence — 'It is better for me to fall into your hands, and not do it, than to sin in the sight of the Lord' — has been quoted for two thousand years as the definition of conscience.

keyVerses.text: And he took a wife, whose name was Susanna, the daughter of Chelcias, a very fair woman, and one that feared the Lord. Her parents also were righteous, and taught their daughter according to the law of Moses.
keyVerses.why: The story stakes everything on formation: her courage in the garden is the fruit of teaching received at home.

keyVerses.text: It is better for me to fall into your hands, and not do it, than to sin in the sight of the Lord.
keyVerses.why: The sentence the whole book exists to carry — conscience choosing the costlier death.

keyVerses.text: And she weeping looked up toward heaven: for her heart trusted in the Lord.
keyVerses.why: Between accusation and sentence, one gesture — the look up that the story sets against the elders who 'turned away their eyes... that they might not look unto heaven' (1:9).

keyVerses.text: From that day forth was Daniel had in great reputation in the sight of the people.
keyVerses.why: The tale works as an origin story: before the lions' den, before the dreams, Daniel's gift for judgment is born in this courtroom.

questions.question: Why does this story appear twice — here and as Daniel 13?
questions.answer: The Greek tradition preserved Susanna in two positions: some manuscripts attach it to Daniel as chapter 13, others circulate it as an independent book — which is what this arrangement does, alongside Bel and the Dragon. The story was simply too loved to be fixed in one place; early Christian art and literature cite it constantly.

questions.question: Is Susanna a historical person?
questions.answer: The tale gives no external anchors — it reads as a didactic story set in the exile's world, the genre of Ruth or Jonah: narrative built to teach. Its truth is the kind fiction can carry: what it shows about lust, power, false witness, and conscience has been recognized as true in every century it has been read.

questions.question: What does the name Susanna mean?
questions.answer: Lily — in Hebrew, Shoshannah. The name fits the story's imagery: a flower in an enclosed garden, desired, trampled by corrupt power, and vindicated. The garden setting itself — innocence walked, watched, and violated — has made the tale a favorite of painters from the Renaissance onward.

questions.question: Why does the story insist the elders 'turned away their eyes... that they might not look unto heaven'?
questions.answer: Because the whole tale turns on seeing. The elders refuse to look up and so lose all judgment; Susanna, accused, looks up to heaven (1:35); Daniel sees what the crowd cannot. The story's quiet theology: corruption begins as averted eyes, and justice begins with looking at God.

questions.question: What did the early church see in this story?
questions.answer: Christ prefigured in the pattern — the innocent condemned by false witnesses and vindicated by resurrection power — which is why it was read at Easter. It also gave the church its earliest arguments for careful judicial process: Hippolytus and others cited Daniel's 'without examination' as a rule. And it gave art history Susanna at her bath, one of the most painted scenes in Western art.
